corpus_definition: A protected area where animals can live safely.
usage_note: Countable noun: a nature reserve, two nature reserves. Usually 'in a nature reserve' or 'visit a nature reserve'. Also called a wildlife reserve.

relations.note: Same meaning; both are protected land for animals and plants.
A safe place for animals, often for birds or animals that are hurt or in danger.
Related: a very large protected area, usually also open for tourists and walking.
Related, but a park in a town is for people, not mainly for wild animals.

context.text: Last spring our class visited a nature reserve near the Chatkal mountains. We were not allowed to make fires, because the nature reserve protects rare birds and snow leopards.

reviewer_note: Fixed noun phrase; no forms. Uzbekistan has the Chatkal reserve, so the context is realistic.

corpus_definition: To find the right direction when traveling to a place.

forms.definition: the skill of finding the way when you travel, using maps or tools
forms.example: The phone's navigation helped us find the hotel in Bukhara.

syn.note: A more technical phrase for working out which way to go.
Related: knowing where you are and which way you are facing.

forms.note: Also used for the menus that help you move around a website: 'site navigation'.

forms.definition: to find which way to go when you travel somewhere
forms.example: We used a map to navigate through the old streets.

syn.note: Easy everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Related: to control which way a car or boat goes.
Related: to show someone else the way.

ant.note: When you get lost, you cannot find the right way.

forms.definition: connected with finding the way, for ships, planes or cars
forms.example: The pilot checked the navigational equipment before take-off.

forms.definition: wide and deep enough for boats to travel on
forms.example: The river is navigable for small boats in spring.
forms.note: Belongs to navigate = sail a ship along a river or sea, not finding your way in general.
There is no common adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who plans the route on a ship, plane or car journey
people.example: In the rally, the navigator reads the map and the driver drives.

context.text: Without a phone, it is hard to navigate in a new city. My uncle still prefers paper maps, but most drivers in Tashkent use navigation apps now.

reviewer_note: navigable kept as other_meaning (boats on rivers); no -ly adverb exists.

forms.definition: something that you must have or that you cannot live without
forms.example: Water is a necessity for every living thing.

syn.note: Easy word: a need is something you must have.
Usually plural: 'basic essentials' like food and soap.
More formal: something that is asked for or needed.
Informal noun: 'A coat is a must in winter.'

ant.note: A luxury is nice to have but you can live without it.

forms.definition: to make something needed or impossible to avoid
forms.example: The heavy snow necessitated closing the schools.

syn.note: More common, still a bit formal.
Less formal: 'This calls for a celebration.'

forms.definition: needed in order to do something or to get a result
forms.example: Is it necessary to book a table at this restaurant?

syn.note: Easy word with the same meaning.
Very important and needed.
Often used for rules: 'required documents'.
Very important, often for life or success.

forms.definition: in a way that cannot be different or avoided
forms.example: Expensive shoes are not necessarily better shoes.

syn.note: Formal: in a way that cannot be stopped.
Related: 'not necessarily' is close to 'not always'.

ant.note: In a way that is not needed: 'He was unnecessarily rude.'

forms.note: Most often used in the negative: 'not necessarily' = not always, maybe not.

context.text: A warm coat is a necessity in Tashkent in January. It is not necessary to buy an expensive one, because expensive clothes are not necessarily warmer.

reviewer_note: No -ity split claimed (necess- is not a word); unnecessary/unnecessarily kept as antonyms.

corpus_definition: to fail to take care of someone or something properly

forms.definition: the state of not being looked after properly
forms.example: The old house fell into neglect after the family moved away.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Related: not being careful; neglect is more about not looking after something for a long time.

ant.note: Care means looking after someone or something well.
Giving attention means noticing and looking after something.

forms.definition: to not look after someone or something as well as you should
forms.example: Don't neglect your health when you work long hours.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Related: to pay no attention to something on purpose.
Related but stronger: to leave someone or something completely.

ant.note: To take care of someone or something.
To make sure someone or something is safe and well.

forms.definition: not looked after, so in a bad state
forms.example: The neglected garden was full of weeds.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little less common.
Related: left completely, with nobody there.
Related: used for buildings in bad condition.

forms.definition: not giving enough care or attention to someone or something
forms.example: He was neglectful of his duties at work.

syn.note: Easy word: not paying enough attention.
More formal: not paying attention.

ant.note: Attentive people notice and look after others well.
Caring people look after others kindly.

forms.note: There is no common adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandfather's vineyard was neglected for years after he got ill. Now my cousins visit every weekend, because they don't want to neglect it again.

reviewer_note: negligent/negligence share an old root but are not made from neglect, so they are not_family.

corpus_definition: A system of many things connected to each other.

forms.definition: a large system of things, people or computers that are connected
forms.example: The city has a good network of buses and metro lines.

syn.note: More general: any set of parts that work together.
A web is a network with many crossing lines.
Related: a network of lines, roads or power cables, often in squares.
Related: a group of shops or hotels owned by one company.

forms.definition: meeting people who can help you in your job
forms.example: Conferences are good for networking.
forms.note: Belongs to network = meet people to help your career, not a system of connected things.

forms.definition: to connect computers or machines so they can share information
forms.example: All the computers in the office are networked.

syn.note: Easy, more general word.
Same idea; often used for computers too.

forms.definition: connected to other computers or machines in one system
forms.example: The school has networked printers on every floor.

syn.note: Easy word with the same meaning.
Same idea, a little more general.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Our school computers are networked, so the teacher can send files to everyone. When the network is down, nobody can print homework.

reviewer_note: network itself is net + work, no affix claimed; networking (career sense) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: Not supporting either side in an argument or war.

forms.definition: the state of not supporting either side in a war or argument
forms.example: Switzerland is famous for its neutrality.

syn.note: Formal: treating both sides the same.
Related: judging only by facts, not feelings.

ant.note: Bias means you support one side unfairly.

forms.definition: to stop something from having an effect
forms.example: The medicine neutralizes the poison.
forms.note: Belongs to neutral = having no effect (as in chemistry), not taking no side. British spelling: neutralise.

forms.definition: not supporting either side in an argument or war
forms.example: The teacher stayed neutral when the two students argued.

syn.note: Formal: treating both sides the same.
Not helping one side unfairly.
Based on facts, not personal feelings.
Related: not controlled by any side.

ant.note: Showing only one side of an argument.

forms.definition: in a way that does not support either side
forms.example: The reporter described the protest neutrally.

syn.note: Formal: in a way that treats both sides the same.
Using facts, not feelings.

context.text: When my two sisters argue, I try to stay neutral. My mother says neutrality is wise, but sometimes I just leave the room.

reviewer_note: neutralize is other_meaning (stop an effect, chemistry), not the taking-no-side meaning.

corpus_definition: A very bad or frightening dream.

forms.definition: a very frightening or unpleasant dream
forms.example: After the horror film, my little brother had a nightmare.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Related: a very strong fear at night, mostly in young children.

forms.note: Also used for a very bad experience: 'The journey was a nightmare.'
There is no verb. People say 'have a nightmare'.

forms.definition: very frightening or unpleasant, like a bad dream
forms.example: We had a nightmarish journey through the snowstorm.

syn.note: Easy word: making you afraid.
Stronger: making you very afraid.
Related: very shocking and unpleasant.

forms.note: There is no common adverb in this family.

context.text: Last night I had a nightmare about missing my exam. It felt so nightmarish that I woke up and checked the clock three times.

reviewer_note: nightmare is not split into night + mare (no compound/affix claimed).

corpus_definition: Having high moral qualities or belonging to a high rank.

forms.definition: the quality of being honest, brave and good; also the highest social class
forms.example: Everyone admired the nobility of her actions.

syn.note: Related: being honest and keeping your promises. US spelling: honor.
Same as the class meaning: the people of the highest rank.

forms.definition: to make someone or something better or more respected
forms.example: Hard work and kindness ennoble a person.

syn.note: Formal: to make something seem more important or respected.

forms.definition: having very good moral qualities, or belonging to a high social rank
forms.example: It was a noble act to give your seat to the old man.

syn.note: Honest and fair. US spelling: honorable.
Related: good enough to be admired.
Related: kind and happy to give.
For the rank meaning: from the highest social class.

ant.note: Not honest or fair; bringing shame. US spelling: dishonorable.

forms.definition: in a brave, honest and good way
forms.example: He nobly gave his prize money to the hospital.

syn.note: In an honest and fair way.
Related: without fear.
Related: in a kind way, giving a lot.

context.text: Helping the flood victims was a noble thing to do. The young volunteers acted nobly and asked for nothing in return.

reviewer_note: nobleman/noblewoman left out (compounds). The corpus definition covers both 'good character' and 'high rank'; one map with both.

usage_note: neither ... nor ...: 'Neither Ali nor Aziz came.' After a negative clause, nor + auxiliary + subject: 'He did not talk, nor did he listen.' Short answer: 'I don't like it.' 'Nor do I.'

relations.note: Related: after not, people often use 'or': 'He doesn't eat meat or fish.'
In short answers 'Neither do I' means the same as 'Nor do I'.
Plainer way to join two negative ideas.

context.text: My brother doesn't like football, nor does he watch it on TV. Neither my father nor my uncle watches it at all.

reviewer_note: Grammar word: kind changed from word to function; inversion after nor is in the usage note.

corpus_definition: A message that tells you about something new.

forms.definition: a message that tells you that something new has happened
forms.example: I got a notification when my parcel arrived at the post office.

syn.note: On phones, an alert is the same as a notification.
More general: any written or spoken information sent to someone.
Related: a message that helps you remember something.
Related: information told to many people.

forms.definition: to tell someone officially about something
forms.example: Please notify the school if your child is ill.

syn.note: Same meaning, a bit formal.
Easy, everyday word.
Easy everyday phrase.
To tell someone quickly about danger or something important.

forms.note: There is no common adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: The bank will notify you when your card is ready. You will get a notification on your phone, so check your messages.

reviewer_note: notice has a similar meaning but is not made from notify, so it is not_family.
